The Forgotten Women Warriors of Japan: The Truth Behind the “Female Samurai”

Popular culture gives the samurai a familiar silhouette: a man, two swords and a private code. Japan’s past is harder to frame. Women defended households, appear in war tales and, in a few extraordinary cases, entered battle themselves—but not every famous image is equally historical.

Researched and edited in Japan by Yuji Shimizu · Published and sources checked November 7, 2026

The phrase “female samurai” is useful because it immediately overturns a stereotype. It is also dangerous. Samurai could describe status, household, service and military function, while women’s positions changed across centuries. There was no single official class called “female samurai” that remained unchanged from the medieval period to the nineteenth century.

A more careful term is onna-musha—a woman warrior. Even that label covers different evidence: a person in a military chronicle, a heroine expanded by later storytellers, a woman defending a siege, or a fighter recorded close to the event. The surprise is not that one secret army of women has been erased. It is that legend, household duty, combat and modern memory have been folded into one glamorous picture.

Tomoe Gozen: the warrior almost everyone recognizes

Tomoe Gozen is the great entrance to the subject. In The Tale of the Heike, the war epic about the conflict between the Taira and Minamoto clans, Tomoe serves Kiso Yoshinaka and is described as a formidable rider and fighter. Later visual culture made her unforgettable: armored, mounted and often carrying a naginata. The Tokyo National Museum’s eighteenth-century Tomoe Gozen Shutsujin-zu, recorded by Japan’s Cultural Heritage Online, shows exactly that commanding form.

But a powerful literary presence is not the same as a securely documented biography. The Yoshinaka Museum notes that Tomoe does not appear in surviving contemporary documents or even in the Kamakura shogunate’s official chronicle, Azuma Kagami. Different versions of the Heike tradition also change her story. Her historical existence therefore remains uncertain.

The central answer: women warriors were not simply invented—but the most famous “female samurai” image combines several different histories. Tomoe is strongest as a literary and artistic memory; Nakano Takeko stands much closer to recoverable event history.

This distinction does not make Tomoe meaningless. Stories influence what later audiences believe courage can look like. Edo-period artists repeatedly pictured her because she gave bravery a striking female body. Yet saying “the sources do not let us prove this” is more respectful than turning a beloved figure into evidence she cannot carry.

The naginata was not always “a woman’s weapon”

The curved blade on a long shaft is now closely associated with women’s martial arts. That association has a history of its own. Research published in 2025 by Chloé Bérard argues that medieval and early-modern sources do not support a simple, timeless bond between samurai women and naginata. In medieval warfare the weapon was used by warriors more broadly. As spears and firearms changed battle, its role also changed.

The strong public link between women and naginata was shaped much later, especially through modern education. Bérard’s earlier research traces how naginata entered girls’ schooling in the early twentieth century and was presented as a distinctly feminine budo. A study of the Women’s Normal College of Nara found that it was taught there from 1911 to 1946, eventually entering the regular curriculum. The weapon’s modern gender image was therefore constructed through schools as well as inherited from warrior memory.

That creates a useful warning for museum visitors. An artwork of a woman holding a naginata may tell us a great deal about the period that produced the artwork, not only the period it claims to portray. Armor can be later, a scene can be literary, and a memorial can preserve community memory without being the battlefield itself.

1868: Nakano Takeko enters the record

Nakano Takeko belongs to another moment entirely. In 1868, the Boshin War brought imperial forces against supporters of the Tokugawa order. Fighting reached Aizu in present-day Fukushima Prefecture. Local official histories remember Takeko as the leader of women who armed themselves and fought with naginata during the conflict.

According to Aizuwakamatsu’s official tourism account, Takeko fought near Yanagi Bridge and died in battle. A memorial erected in 1938 stands near the site. Aizubange Town, where her grave is located, also preserves materials about her life. The details have passed through commemoration and later retelling, but the documentary situation is fundamentally different from Tomoe’s: Takeko is attached to named relatives, locations, a nineteenth-century conflict and continuing local records.

Her group is commonly called the Jōshitai, or women’s unit. The neat name can make it sound like a normal official regiment. It was not. The women formed and fought in extraordinary circumstances, when the accepted military structure did not offer them an ordinary place. That tension is part of the story: courage did not erase the limits placed on them.

The paper tied to her weapon

Aizuwakamatsu’s official account says that Takeko tied a death poem to her naginata before departing. The poem compares her own body with the fierce heart of a warrior. In the manga above, the narrow white paper appears in the first panel as a mystery and returns in the last. It was not a lucky ribbon or decoration. It carried a declaration of resolve.

The poem is remembered at Takeko’s memorial. Yet readers should notice the layers: the battle occurred in 1868; the monument was erected seventy years later; and today’s visitor meets the past through both site and commemoration. History is not weakened by naming those layers. It becomes easier to see what survives, what was rebuilt and what a later community chose to honor.

The real correction is not “samurai were secretly women too.” It is that military history looks different when households, stories, sieges, education and memory enter the frame.

What films and games usually compress

A screen warrior needs to be read in seconds. A blade, armor and fearless pose do the work. Real lives are less efficient. Status did not guarantee battlefield command. Training did not mean constant combat. A woman could belong to a warrior household without living the adventure imagined by modern fiction. At the same time, excluding women from the picture simply because most formal armies were male also distorts the record.

The better comparison is not myth versus truth, as if only one can matter. Ask what kind of truth each source offers. A war tale reveals the heroic language of its tradition. A print reveals later visual appetite. A local record and grave connect a person to place. A school curriculum reveals how modern Japan remade an old weapon into gendered education.

How to follow the story in Japan

In Aizuwakamatsu, Tsuruga Castle provides the larger setting for the 1868 siege, while the Nakano Takeko memorial near Yanagi Bridge and her grave at Hōkaiji in Aizubange connect the story to specific places. Treat the memorial as a place of remembrance, not a stage for battle poses. Check local transport and temple access before visiting; a grave is not an entertainment attraction.

For Tomoe, begin with surviving art and texts rather than searching for a single authenticated battlefield biography. Cultural Heritage Online provides the Tokyo National Museum record for the eighteenth-century painting. The Yoshinaka Museum explores how stories about Kiso Yoshinaka and Tomoe developed, while openly stating the limits of the historical evidence.

The Japanese terms make those distinctions easier to notice. Practice 女武者 (onna-musha, woman warrior), 薙刀 (naginata) and the N2 structures used in the manga through the free, no-signup Japanese Training Lab.

Remember the women—and the uncertainty

Tomoe Gozen and Nakano Takeko should not be flattened into interchangeable “female samurai.” One comes to us chiefly through literature and later art; the other through the violent end of the samurai era and the local memory of Aizu. Their distance from each other is what makes the history richer.

Women warriors matter not because they prove a modern slogan about the past. They matter because they force better questions. Who counted as a warrior? Who was permitted to fight? Who was remembered in official records, and who survived through stories? Once those questions begin, the familiar samurai silhouette can no longer stand alone.
